newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria party vote will not help economy - papers.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria party vote will not help economy - papers.

text.p: Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's narrow victory over his party critics in a confidence vote has bought him time but will not bring an end to Bulgaria's economic crisis any nearer, newspapers said on Wednesday.

A marathon 20-hour meeting called to discuss calls for cabinet changes and policy reform ended with a confidence vote on Tuesday in which 87 members of the party leadership backed Videnov, 69 voted against him and two abstained.
"Eighteen Socialists saved Zhan and buried Bulgaria deeper," said the Standart, while Night Trud ran with the headline "Videnov stays, Bulgaria goes".
The meeting of the party's supreme council made no cabinet changes and Videnov said any reshuffle would be discussed at a full party congress scheduled for December 21 and 22.

The party also gave its support for Videnov to seek implementation of a currency board proposed by the International Monetary Fund to halt the collapse of the Bulgarian currency and stabilise the economy.
But commentators dismissed the move, which has been used by other countries to restore confidence and help defeat hyperinflation, as a cover for the Socialists' own lack of economic policy.
"The currency board is very convenient for all politicians, by placing the country in receivership, the IMF spares the parties the need to think and to govern," said 24 Hours.
The lev, which started the year at 70 to the dollar, touched 260 on Wednesday.
The opposition Union of Democratic Forces says it will press for early general elections whether a currency board is introduced or not.
Michael Deppler, deputy director of the IMF's European department, left Sofia on Tuesday. The IMF said technical missions would follow to discuss details of the currency board.
A currency board must be approved by parliament, where the Socialists are half way through their four-year term.

The IMF has twice postponed a badly-needed $115 million credit due to Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets. Agreement with the Fund is vital if the Balkan state is to avoid defaulting on its $10 billion foreign debt.
The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions plans a one-day general strike on December 4 to protest against falling living standards.
